For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

text.text: The aim of this study was to explore the interrelationship between cognitive polyphasia and cognitive dissonance in the management of contradictions.
We argue that both concepts maintain a circular relationship.

To support this position, we establish a theoretical path structured around four core axes: 1) the recognition that Festinger and his followers already considered dissonance management mechanisms that, much like cognitive polyphasia, maintain inconsistency; 2) from a diachronic perspective, dissonance can stem from cognitive polyphasia; 3) from a synchronic perspective, the varieties of cognitive polyphasia can be systematized within the functional approach to cognitive dissonance; 4) this systematization raises questions regarding the self and identity, bringing Social Representations Theory closer to contemporary models of the self.
Throughout this path, we outline an integrative model for the study of inconsistency management, offering brief considerations on the challenges that future research must overcome.

text.text: As a way of overcoming the limitations of models that reduced dissonance to a mere motivational state, Kelman and Baron (1968b) advanced a functional analysis of inconsistency.

text.text: For these authors, inconsistency is initially perceived as a signal that activates a search process aimed at evaluating its implications.
When this evaluation reveals no threat to goals, values, or coping resources, no further response is elicited.
When, however, relevant functional implications are identified, individuals may reduce the resulting tension without necessarily eliminating the inconsistency itself.

On this basis, the model systematizes responses to contradiction according to two combinable dimensions: the nature of the process mobilized (avoidance or confrontation) and the nature of the outcome achieved (reduction or maintenance).
Based on this framework, Kelman and Baron (1968a) identified fourteen distinct mechanisms: eight oriented toward inconsistency reduction and six toward its maintenance.

text.text: These mechanisms are distributed across avoidance and confrontation processes, yielding four reduction-avoidance mechanisms and four reduction-confrontation mechanisms, as well as three maintenance-avoidance modes and three maintenance-confrontation modes.
Their model therefore constitutes a conceptually robust formulation capable of accounting for both the elimination and the preservation of contradiction over time.
For the purposes of the present study, particular attention is given to mechanisms of inconsistency maintenance.

Reduction mechanisms, regardless of the process involved, culminate in the outcomes' characteristic of CDT in its classical formulationnamely, the elimination of contradiction and the restoration of consonance.

Maintenance mechanisms, by contrast, make it possible to understand how the tension associated with inconsistency may be regulated without eliminating the contradiction itself, thereby opening space for the coexistence of incompatible rationalities.

text.text: As Kolakowski (1963) argues, "our lives are lived under the strain of contradictory loyalties" (p. 208), requiring situated choices without the complete rejection of the alternatives set aside.
Diachronic polyphasia thus describes the sociocultural background against which cognitive conflicts become possible, even if they are not continuously activated.
Although this perspective does not focus on ongoing cognitive conflicts, it encompasses the societal and cultural conditions that make them possible.
Since cognitive dissonance emerges following decisions made in contexts of conflict, diachronic cognitive polyphasia provides the conditions for its possibility.

text.text: Adopting the language of sets, Mikael-Silva (2024) examined under what conditions two or more explanatory systems could coexist without collapsing the Flat Earthers' regime of truth.
Faced with the incompatibility between modern astronomy and biblical cosmology, the two sets could not be simultaneously true.
Since maintaining biblical literalism functioned as a long-term goal, modern science was consequently displaced as "false."
When the dilemma involved distinct religious cosmologies, such as the biblical and the indigenous Cherokee ones, considering one false would compromise the veracity of the other.
The recurrent solution was hybridization, preserving both united within the same category.

Conversely, specific contradictions -such as the critique of "unobservable" scientific entities coexisting with the defense of an "invisible dome"were managed through compartmentalization, keeping "true beliefs" and "true observations" in parallel sets.

Both models emerge as a response to two classic limitations in group studies: the focus on a single salient social identity (Becker et al., 2023) or a single ingroup-outgroup categorization (Roccas & Brewer, 2002), and the scant attention paid to intraindividual processes (Amiot et al., 2007; Becker et al., 2023).

text.text: The model we adapt for the study of contradiction management aims not only to overcome these limitations but also to systematically integrate the advances of this literature on the self and identity into the framework of inconsistency mechanisms.

In order to delineate the scope of the contributions of an integrative model of contradiction management, we explicate its theoretical implications, its analytical boundaries, and the questions that remain open.
First, this approach appears particularly suited to specific types of social groups and contradictions, especially so-called crosscutting groups.

According to Roccas and Brewer (2002), these groups emerge when different dimensions of classification and membership do not fully coincide, such that individuals defined as an ingroup on one dimension may be an outgroup on another.

text.text: As previously argued, the frantic encounter between different forms of knowledge, cultural pluralization, and the coexistence of multiple symbolic authorities (Jovchelovitch, 2008a; Giddens, 2012) make membership in crosscutting groups increasingly common.

text.text: In a study on conflicts experienced by obstetrician-gynecologists, for instance, both abortion providers and conscientious objectors reported tension between professional and religious identities when faced with requests for legal abortion (Mikael-Silva et al., 2025).

text.text: However, unlike the objectors, the providers tended to compartmentalize the medical and the religious/spiritual viewpoints, activating them depending on the context.
Another example is Mikael-Silva's (2024) study on Flat Earth YouTube channels, which included a PhD in geophysics and a Master's graduate in Intelligence and Security.

These YouTubers belonged to the institutional scientific community while simultaneously advocating for a Flat Earth, managing the contradictions between academic affiliation and conspiracy adherence through x.15 mechanisms of inconsistency maintenance, most notably compartmentalization.

Regarding contradictions, we suggest paying closer attention to inconsistencies between: a) norms and social or personal identity; b) one or more identities and identifications; c) perspectives and positions adopted by the same individual; d) antagonistic social practices within the same subject or group; e) competing knowledge systems or regimes of truth.
Each of these forms of contradiction stems from potential interactions among the normative, identity, epistemic, positional, and practical levels.
This enumeration, however, does not intend to exhaust the phenomenon but rather to indicate initial analytical axes that can be refined and structured in future investigations.

To systematize the analytical axes involved in the emergence and management of contradictions within plural contexts, we propose a multilevel model that articulates societal, social, cross-cutting, situational, operational, and functional dimensions (Table 2).
text.formatted: To systematize the analytical axes involved in the emergence and management of contradictions within plural contexts, we propose a multilevel model that articulates societal, social, cross-cutting, situational, operational, and functional dimensions (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: These levels are structured from the broader historical, sociocultural, and institutional conditions down to the situated mechanisms of inconsistency management and their regulatory effects.

By explicating the processual contribution of each level, the table organizes the phenomenon of inconsistency not as an isolated cognitive failure, but as an institutional and dynamic product of contemporary social life.
The societal level implies that culturally plural and hybrid societies, marked by multiple authorities, tend to exhibit greater conflict and conditions that favor diachronic cognitive polyphasia.
These same conditions foster the coexistence of cross-cutting groups at the social level.

Since groups are sources of norms, social identities, epistemologies, positions, and practices, the cross-cutting nature of these memberships and axes generates potential inter-level tensions and contradictions (cross-cutting level).

At the situational level, the need to manage these contradictions may depend on the salience of one or more identities within a given context, situational demands, individual and group goals, and the communication systems that organize how contradictions are framed, potentially stimulating synchronic cognitive polyphasia.

Once activated, the operational level predicts that individuals and groups will mobilize mechanisms of contradiction reduction or maintenance, the effects of which are simultaneously functional and systemic: functional, because they regulate knowledge and social representations, conflicts between group memberships, and inconsistencies that threaten the self, self-concept, and identity; and systemic, because the outcomes of inconsistency management reverberate through higher levels, feeding back into new social configurations and contradictions (García Canclini, 2005).

text.text: In Amiot et al. (2019) study, for instance, the differentiation and hierarchization among animal categories (pets, farm animals, wild animals, predators, pests) facilitated their compartmentalization, thereby aiding in the reduction of dissonance associated with morally ambiguous relationships.

Although that study did not formally distinguish between these mechanisms, it highlights the linkage among compartmentalization, differentiationunderstood as the separation of elements into distinct categories to confront contradictionand displacement (hierarchization).

Similarly, parallels established with Kelman and Baron's (1968a) model reveal relevant convergences: Roccas and Brewer (2002) associated intersection with differentiation, dominance with bolsteringemphasizing the positive aspects of the inconsistent behavior to overshadow the contradiction -and merger with transcendenceevoking a higher-order principle in whose name the inconsistency ceases to be perceived as such.
In our proposal, merger aligns closely with hybridization; nonetheless, the comparison with transcendence reinforces the interdependence of these processes, which can operate jointly.
Identifying the conditions under which each mechanism is deployed.
The use of these mechanisms varies according to context, goals, and social functions.
Although Kelman and Baron (1968a) suggested general conditions, it remains necessary to specify the psychosociological factors that predict the choice of each strategy.

Amiot et al. (2017b) offer a promising avenue by demonstrating, within a sports context, that the manipulation of normative legitimacy affects the need for compartmentalization: hostile behaviors directed at the opposing team were more heavily compartmentalized when perceived as illegitimate.
This type of experimental design can contribute significantly to refining the proposed hypotheses.
Promoting dialogue with different theories of the self.
While SRT has converged with Dialogical Self Theory, CDT has engaged more intensely with intergroup models.

The notion of perspective may constitute a point of convergence between these traditions, as it is present in both Festinger and Moscovici and forms part of the broader vocabulary of Social Psychology (Graumann, 1994; Priego-Hernández, 2017).

text.text: In this study, we have argued for a circular relationship between cognitive polyphasia and cognitive dissonance.

Even before Moscovici formulated the notion of cognitive polyphasia, Festinger (1957) already recognized different ways of coping with dissonance, which were subsequently systematized by Kelman and Baron (1968a).
text.formatted: Even before Moscovici formulated the notion of cognitive polyphasia, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Festinger (1957)</ref> already recognized different ways of coping with dissonance, which were subsequently systematized by <ref type="bibr">Kelman and Baron (1968a)</ref>.

text.text: By encompassing both reduction and maintenance mechanisms of inconsistency, their model parsimoniously accommodates the synchronic manifestations of cognitive polyphasia.

Only selective prevalence appears conceptually redundant and can be subsumed under compartmentalization, the ramifications of which bring SRT and CDT closer to more robust formulations of the self and identity.

Building upon this trajectory, we have also proposed an integrative systematization for the study of inconsistency management within the scope of SRT, outlining analytical axes and research challenges.
Our proposal offers a complementary contribution by bridging intra-and interpersonal levels while simultaneously expanding the study of cognitive dissonance to intraand intergroup levels.

In addition to strengthening the investigation of intrapersonal conflicts associated with multiple group memberships and their effects on the self, this model allows for a more precise examination of the different modes of managing inconsistency.
Despite these contributions, certain limitations must be acknowledged.

First, we focused our analysis on the articulation between cognitive polyphasia and cognitive dissonance; a broader dialogue between these traditions exceeds the scope of this article, having been explored in greater depth in another work (Mikael-Silva, 2024).

text.text: Second, we restricted ourselves to three inconsistency maintenance mechanisms, relegating other processes proposed by Kelman and Baron (1968a) to the background -a more detailed study of which could expand and refine the model presented here.

text.text: Third, it remains necessary to broaden the dialogue with other approaches within SRT, different formulations of CDT, and other social psychology theories that can strengthen, strain, or revise the proposed framework.

Finally, our proposal adopts an integrative orientation that does not always find consensus within social psychology, particularly regarding the intersection of SRT and intraindividual cognitive processes.
This debate, however, is already present within the SRT tradition itself, especially in its structural approach.

Here, we share the stance of Rateau et al. (2012), who remind us that although social representations are collective constructions situated between the social and the individual, they are still partially elaborated by individuals.

Because the SICM does not explain how these representations change over time, Amiot et al. (2007) proposed a Cognitive-Developmental Model (CDM), grounded in intergroup models and neo-Piagetian assumptions.

The model outlines four stages of identity integration: a) anticipatory categorization, where integration begins with the anticipation and projection of a new role; b) categorization, the point at which distinct identities are recognized and their associated values and norms become salient, dichotomously reinforcing group membership and identification; c) compartmentalization, a phase in which multiple old and new identities are recognized and compartmentalized within the self, remaining context-dependent; d) integration, a stage where multiple social identities become superordinately integrated within the global self-concept, reducing their contextual dependence.
